meta.title: UK general elections, 1802-2024
sources: Wikipedia general election articles (seats, leaders, dates)

eras.label: The Unreformed Commons
eras.blurb: Before the Great Reform Act, elections were contests of patronage more than votes: rotten boroughs, tiny electorates and hundreds of uncontested seats. Governments were made and unmade in Parliament, not at the polls.

eras.label: Reform and Realignment
eras.blurb: The 1832 Reform Act began the slow expansion of the franchise. Whigs and Tories fractured over Corn Laws and free trade, re-forming as the Liberal and Conservative parties by mid-century.

eras.label: The Mass Franchise
eras.blurb: Gladstone and Disraeli made elections national duels, Ireland made them existential, and successive Reform Acts tripled the electorate. By 1910 the Lords, Home Rule and a rising Labour movement had brought the constitutional order to a breaking point.

eras.label: Labour's Rise
eras.blurb: The 1918 franchise revolution enfranchised women and working-class men, Sinn Féin swept Ireland out of Westminster, and Labour displaced the divided Liberals within a decade. Depression-era crises produced the century's biggest landslides.

eras.label: The Postwar Settlement
eras.blurb: Attlee's 1945 landslide built the welfare state; the Conservatives governed for thirteen years without dismantling it. Two-party dominance peaked, with Labour and the Conservatives together taking nine of every ten votes.

eras.label: Crisis and Thatcherism
eras.blurb: Two elections in 1974 delivered hung-parliament instability and a strong third-party vote. Thatcher's three victories remade the political economy while the opposition split, and FPTP turned a divided anti-Conservative vote into 18 years of Tory rule.

eras.label: New Labour
eras.blurb: Blair's 1997 landslide began thirteen years of Labour government, devolution and a supreme era of electoral professionalisation, ending in the first hung parliament and first formal coalition since the war.

eras.label: The Brexit Realignment
eras.blurb: Four elections in nine years, framed by two referendums. Old class loyalties dissolved: the SNP swept Scotland, the Red Wall fell in 2019, and in 2024 FPTP produced the most disproportional result in British history.

elections.summary: The first election of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, after the Acts of Union brought 100 Irish members to Westminster. Addington's ministry, having delivered peace with France at Amiens, was comfortably sustained.

Held months after Pitt the Younger's death, with Grenville's 'Ministry of All the Talents' in office. The broad coalition strengthened its position, but would fall within a year over Catholic emancipation.
The Duke of Portland's Pittites won a decisive majority on a 'No Popery' cry after the King dismissed the Talents over Catholic relief. Anti-Catholicism proved a reliable electoral weapon.
Fought during war with Napoleon and America under Lord Liverpool, months after Spencer Perceval became the only British PM ever assassinated. Liverpool consolidated the long Tory ascendancy.
Post-Waterloo distress and radical agitation eroded but did not end Liverpool's majority. The Whigs gained ground for the first time in a decade.
Triggered by George III's death, held amid the Peterloo aftermath and the Cato Street Conspiracy to murder the cabinet. Liverpool's Tories were returned comfortably.
Liverpool's final election, with Catholic emancipation the dominant question. The Tories held their majority but the issue was now splitting them from within.

George IV's death forced an election as reform agitation surged. Wellington's Tories lost ground, he lost a confidence vote within months, and Earl Grey formed the Whig ministry that would carry the Reform Act.
A de facto referendum on Grey's Reform Bill after it stalled in the Commons. Pro-reform Whigs swept the open constituencies, giving Grey the mandate that forced the bill through the following year.

The first election under the Great Reform Act: rotten boroughs abolished, industrial towns enfranchised and the electorate expanded by roughly half. Grey's Whigs won an overwhelming mandate for the reformed system.

Peel's Tamworth Manifesto, issued for this campaign, founded modern Conservatism as a creed of reform-accepting stability. He gained around 100 seats but fell short, and Melbourne's Whigs returned with Irish and Radical support.
Victoria's accession required the last accession-triggered general election. Melbourne's Whigs held on with a shrinking majority, increasingly dependent on O'Connell's Irish members.
Peel's Conservatives won the first clear opposition-to-majority victory of the reformed era, a landmark in party government. Within five years he would split the party by repealing the Corn Laws.
The first election after the Corn Law schism, with Conservatives divided between Protectionists and Peelites. Russell's Whigs governed from a minority as famine ravaged Ireland.
Derby's minority Conservatives, still committed to protection, narrowly outpolled a fractured opposition. The hung result produced the Aberdeen coalition of Whigs and Peelites within months.
Effectively a plebiscite on Palmerston after Parliament censured him over the bombardment of Canton. The country backed Palmerston emphatically, punishing his Radical and Peelite critics.
Derby's Conservatives gained but fell short again. Weeks later Whigs, Peelites and Radicals met at Willis's Rooms to unite behind Palmerston, the founding moment of the Liberal Party.
Palmerston's last hurrah, won months before his death. His passing unlocked the parliamentary reform question he had suppressed, setting up the Second Reform Act.

The first election under Disraeli's 1867 Reform Act, which had nearly doubled the electorate to include urban working men. Gladstone's Liberals won decisively on a promise to disestablish the Irish church.
Disraeli won the first outright Conservative majority since 1841, aided by newly organised party machinery and suburban 'villa Toryism'. Gladstone temporarily retired, calling the defeat a release.
Gladstone's Midlothian campaign, the first modern stump-speaking tour, turned foreign policy morality into a mass electoral cause and swept Disraeli from office. Campaigning would never be the same.
The first election after the Third Reform Act extended the household franchise to the counties and redrew the whole constituency map. Parnell's Irish Party won 86 seats and held the balance of power.
Fought on Gladstone's first Home Rule Bill, which had split the Liberals. Salisbury's Conservatives and the breakaway Liberal Unionists won decisively, beginning two decades of Unionist dominance.
Gladstone returned at 82 for a fourth premiership, governing in minority with Irish support. His second Home Rule Bill passed the Commons but died in the Lords.
Salisbury's Unionists crushed a demoralised Liberal Party a year after Gladstone's retirement. The Conservative-Liberal Unionist alliance now governed as a single electoral force.
Called at the high tide of Boer War patriotism, an early example of an opportunistic wartime dissolution. Salisbury held his majority; a young Labour Representation Committee won its first two seats.

A Liberal landslide fuelled by tariff reform splits, 'Chinese slavery' and nonconformist anger over education. The Conservatives fell to 156 seats, and 29 Labour members arrived as a parliamentary force.

elections.label: January 1910
elections.knownAs: The Peers versus the People election
elections.summary: Fought over Lloyd George's People's Budget after the Lords rejected it, breaking constitutional convention. Asquith lost his majority and governed with Irish support, the price of which was Home Rule.

elections.label: December 1910
elections.summary: A second election in one year to force the Parliament Act, with the King's secret pledge to create peers if the Lords resisted. The near-identical result gave Asquith his mandate; the Lords' veto was broken in 1911.

government.note: The Conservatives and Prime Minister David Lloyd George's wing of the Liberal Party contested the 1918 General Election as a Coalition. More than half of House of Commons seats were won by Conservative candidates, so that the subsequent Coalition government was Conservative dominated. Majority of 283 is calculated including the 73 Sinn Fein Members who did not take their seats.

elections.summary: Held days after the Armistice under a transformed franchise: all men over 21 and most women over 30, tripling the electorate. Lloyd George's couponed coalition swept Britain while Sinn Féin swept Ireland and never took its seats.
The Conservatives, having ditched Lloyd George at the Carlton Club, won alone under Bonar Law. Labour became the official opposition for the first time, overtaking the divided Liberals for good.

government.note: Although the Conservatives won the most seats (though not a majority), Labour formed a government after the 1923 election.

elections.summary: Baldwin dissolved early seeking a tariff mandate and lost his majority. Though the Conservatives remained largest, MacDonald formed the first ever Labour government with Liberal acquiescence.

Labour's first government fell within months; the campaign closed amid the forged Zinoviev letter scare. Baldwin won a huge majority and the Liberals collapsed to 40 seats, confirming two-party politics.

The first election with equal franchise for women at 21, dubbed for that reason the Flapper election. Labour became the largest party for the first time and MacDonald formed his second minority government on the eve of the Depression.

government.note: Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald led a 'National Government' into the 1931 election which consisted of the Conservative and Liberal parties along with a few National Labour Members like MacDonald.  Conservatives won over three quarters of seats so that the National Government was Conservative dominated.

elections.summary: MacDonald, expelled by his own party for forming a National Government in the financial crisis, led it to the largest landslide in British electoral history: 554 seats and two-thirds of the vote. Labour was reduced to 52.

government.note: The Conservatives contested the 1935 election again as part of a National Government.  The Prime Minister before and after the election, Stanley Baldwin, was a Conservative.  The National Government remained Conservative dominated as over half of House of Commons seats were won by Conservative candidates.

elections.summary: Baldwin's National Government retained a huge majority in the last election before the war. Attlee, initially a stopgap leader, rebuilt Labour to 154 seats; no election followed for ten years.
The wartime coalition dissolved and Labour won its first majority, a landslide that stunned Churchill weeks after victory in Europe. The Attlee government built the NHS and the postwar welfare state.
Attlee's majority collapsed to five on a record-high turnout of nearly 84%. The exhausted government limped on for eighteen months.
Labour polled its highest vote share ever, and more votes than the Conservatives, yet lost: FPTP's most famous inversion. Churchill returned to Downing Street at 76.
Eden, newly succeeding Churchill, became the last PM to increase a governing majority immediately on taking office until 2019. Calm prosperity made it one of the quietest campaigns of the century.
Macmillan's 'never had it so good' era delivered a third successive Conservative victory with an enlarged majority of 100. Commentators wondered if Labour could ever win again.

Wilson ended thirteen years of Conservative rule by four seats, framing Labour as the party of the 'white heat' of technology against a grouse-moor establishment. The tiny majority made a second election inevitable.
Wilson converted his sliver into a majority of nearly 100, the validation election template later used in 1974 and hoped for in 2017. Labour appeared, briefly, hegemonic.
Heath defied virtually every poll to win outright, the biggest opinion-poll failure until 1992. It was the first election with 18-year-olds voting.

elections.label: February 1974
elections.summary: Heath called a snap election on 'Who governs Britain?' during the miners' strike and three-day week; the country answered ambiguously. The first hung parliament since 1929 ended with Wilson governing in minority after coalition talks failed.

elections.label: October 1974
elections.summary: Wilson's validation election, the second of the year, produced a majority of just three. The winter's two campaigns marked the peak of Liberal and SNP insurgency and the end of majority-rule certainty.

After the Winter of Discontent and the first no-confidence defeat of a government since 1924, Thatcher won a 43-seat majority. It began 18 years of Conservative rule and the market revolution that bears her name.

Thatcher, transformed by the Falklands, won a 144-seat landslide over Foot's Labour, whose manifesto was famously called the longest suicide note in history. The SDP-Liberal Alliance took a quarter of the vote but only 23 seats.
A third successive Thatcher victory with the majority barely dented, sealing the Thatcherite settlement. Kinnock's modernisation of Labour had begun but had years to run.

Major won the most votes ever cast for a British party against poll predictions of a hung parliament, the 'Sheffield rally' election. The victory proved poisoned: Black Wednesday broke the government's reputation within months.

Blair's New Labour ended 18 years of Conservative government with a 179-seat majority, the party's largest ever. The Conservatives fell to their worst result of the century and were wiped out in Scotland and Wales.
A near-exact rerun of 1997 on a sharply lower turnout of 59%, the lowest since 1918. Hague resigned immediately; the quiet campaign was punctured only by Prescott's punch.

Blair won a historic third Labour term with a reduced majority, the Iraq war having cut deep into the party's vote. Labour's 35.2% remains the lowest winning share ever converted into a comfortable majority.

government.note: The Conservatives were the largest party following the 2010 election but did not have a majority.  A coalition government was formed with the Liberal Democrats.

elections.summary: The expenses-scandal election and the first with televised leaders' debates produced the first hung parliament since 1974. Cameron and Clegg formed the first full coalition government since the war.

Cameron won the majority the polls said was impossible as the Liberal Democrats collapsed from 57 seats to 8 and the SNP took 56 of Scotland's 59. The result triggered the EU referendum promised in the Conservative manifesto.
May's snap election to strengthen her Brexit hand instead destroyed her majority, as Corbyn's Labour surged. The DUP's ten MPs propped up the government through two years of parliamentary deadlock.
Johnson's 'Get Brexit Done' campaign demolished Labour's Red Wall and delivered an 80-seat majority, the largest Conservative win since 1987. Labour fell to its fewest seats since 1935.

parties.name: Green Party of England and Wales

elections.summary: Starmer's Labour won 411 seats on just 33.7% of the vote, the most disproportional result in British history, as Reform UK split the right and the Conservatives fell to 121 seats, their worst ever. Five parties took over a million votes each.
